Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives: Reduce cheatgrass distribution by applying OUST
Planned_Implementation:
The need exists to reduce the post-fire spread of cheatgrass in order to aid in
the recovery of the overall vegetation community. Cheatgrass is characterized as highly flammable and
highly competitive within specific environments, due to its life history and growth characteristics. High
sunlight and warm soils result after the passage of fire, especially \when soils are degraded or \when fire
frequency has been relatively high. These factors have been found to contribute to the spread and
abundance of non-native species such as cheatgrass.
Cheatgrass further contributes to high fire frequencies, loss of species diversity within native shrub and
perennial grass systems, and decreases in remaining unburned patches as it creates a continuous fuel
bed. Reducing cheatgrass will reduce the risk of hazardous fuels accumulation along roads and
railroads. Cheatgrass is susceptible to control by the application of the herbicide "Oust" (Sulfometuron
Methyl), an approved chemical for use on public lands. The expected fuel bed without implementation
of the proposed action would be exotic and invasive.
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial spraying OUST herbicide on 3,904 acres of rangeland. The OUST herbicide was applied at the 1 ounce per acre rate with 6 gallons of water per acres to control cheatgrass. The project was started on 10/17/1000 and completed on 10/18/2000.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: 9/29/2003: weeds were controlled, preventing further establishment throughout the area.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Wildfire has had a long history influencing sagebrush steppe communities, such communities depend upon climate, topography, and other environmental factors (Tisdale and Hironaka 1981&* West 1996), and wildfire will continue to guide these communities with future lightning and human-caused ignitions.  However, recent and dramatic changes in fire behavior and resulting fire effects have occurred.  As a result and to a greater consequence, the resulting vegetation structure and function will continue to direct future fire-frequency, behavior, season, and magnitude (Clark 1990).  Recent and dramatic changes in the magnitude and frequency of fire=s influence across many areas of sagebrush steppe vegetation have resulted in mono-typic stands of cheatgrass creating more fire-prone/fire-adapted landscapes (Whisenant 1990, Knick and Rotenberry 1997), including the majority of the Big Desert located in eastern Idaho.
  
Nearly 589,941 acres of Federal, State, and private lands across the Big Desert have burned under severe wildfire conditions within the last 4 years (1996-2000).  On July 26, 2000, three more major wildfires were ignited by lightning strikes across this same general area.  These fires were contained largely on land administered by BLM=s Idaho Falls Field Office (IFFO). This Rehabilitation Plan presents information pertinent to all fires and outlines how the efforts may be combined to improve efficiencies.  

Fire Name		Total Acers	BLM Acers	State Acres	Private Acres
Flat Top		57,477 	41,943 	 2,131		13,402
Coffee Point		72,783		69,141 	 1,850		  1,792
Tin Cup		18,140 	  5,649		     0       	      0     
Total Acres		148,400 	116,733	3,981		15,194		


 
Since 1996, approximately 76 percent of the total 590,417 acres of sagebrush steppe within the Big Desert has been impacted by severe wildfire behavior. Many of the total burned acres have undergone recent increases in recorded fire frequency of up to 3 - 4 fires within a 10-year period.  This pattern of repeated large-scale fires across previously impacted areas within relatively short intervals is attributed primarily, to recent cheatgrass invasions across many areas which used to support sagebrush steppe vegetation.  These conditions represent serious fire and resource management concerns. (Please refer to the Big Desert 2000 Rehabilitation Maps across Land Ownership and Key Sage grouse Habitat (Figure I, III)).

Besides reestablishing the vegetation lost during the fire, two other major concerns exist for resource managers and specialists: 

1)  A pattern of repeated fires across previously impacted areas within relatively short time intervals (i.e. high fire frequencies or short fire return intervals) is associated with the recent invading spread of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum), a highly volatile flashy fuel.  

2) The productivity and ecological health of public lands administered by the IFFO is in danger of being severely reduced by invasions of new noxious weeds and the uncontrolled spread of established weeds. 

Vegetation recovery.  The three fires analyzed within this document burned relatively completely with minimal unburned patches of sagebrush steppe vegetation.  The Flat Top Fire burned the most completely of the three, leaving only very small, remnant sagebrush patches.  The Coffee Point Fire burned and left a few larger patches, however many individuals burned lightly within them.  The Tin Cup Fire burned across a smaller area with few larger unburned patches.  The patterns showing such complete burns, at the scale they occurred, represent large and severe landscape impacts, as opposed to smaller, patchy mosaics that allow for diverse vegetation structure with abundant unburned islands to provide for sagebrush steppe recovery.

Areas of poorer ecological condition have been identified where rehabilitation efforts (cheatgrass reduction/control and re-seeding) would provide desirable perennial vegetation to reduce significant soil erosion.  The proposed action would also provide for restoration of the sagebrush steppe ecosystem, associated wildlife habitat, and improvement of other general resource values.  Sagebrush cover needs to be reestablished as soon as possible to meet sage grouse habitat requirements.  Strategically placed fire breaks (i.e. green stripping) are needed to reduce the potential for large fires in the future&* such an action will reduce the spread and heat intensity of a future fire and provide for defensible control features across areas of high potential ignition.



 
Cheatgrass invasion. The need exists to reduce the post-fire spread of cheatgrass in order to aid in the recovery of the overall vegetation community.  Cheatgrass is characterized as highly flammable and highly competitive within specific environments, due to its life history and growth characteristics.  High sunlight and warm soils result after the passage of fire, especially when soils are degraded or when fire frequency has been relatively high.  These factors have been found to contribute to the spread and abundance of non-native species such as cheatgrass.  

Cheatgrass further contributes to high fire frequencies, loss of species diversity within native shrub and perennial grass systems, and decreases in remaining unburned patches as it creates a continuous fuel bed.  Reducing cheatgrass will reduce the risk of hazardous fuels accumulation along roads and railroads.  Cheatgrass is susceptible to control by the application of the herbicide Oust@ (Sulfometuron Methyl), an approved chemical for use on public lands.  The expected fuel bed without implementation of the proposed action would be exotic and invasive. 

Noxious weeds.  The productivity and ecological health of public lands may also be severely reduced by new invasions of noxious weeds and the uncontrolled spread of established weeds.  It is believed that most noxious weeds are initially established on public lands from seeds that are brought in by vehicles, hay, heavy equipment, birds, livestock, wildlife or contaminated seed.  The weeds usually invade and first establish in disturbed areas such as roadsides or heavily grazed rangeland.  Among the noxious weeds of concern are white top, diffuse knapweed, spotted knapweed, leafy spurge, Dalmatian toadflax, scotch thistle, musk thistle, Canadian thistle, tamarisk, and purple loosestrife.  New noxious weeds may be added to the list if they are discovered on public lands in the resource area  (Some weed species, such as halogeton and sandbur, are not listed to-date in the Idaho Noxious Weed Law.). 

The IFFO is committed to employing an integrated weed management program using a variety of methods to achieve effective, safe, economical weed control, including: chemical herbicides, biological agents, prescribed burning methods, seeding to rehabilitate disturbed areas, pulling or digging, public education, management as a tool, and monitoring.  Small infestations can most effectively be treated by the immediate application of herbicides and/or mechanical or manual digging.   Persistently perfecting the program over several months or years is essential as various procedures are integrated and knowledge increases. 

Finally, some roads disturbed through fire suppression activities will need to be improved for continued public access.  Fire suppression funds will be used for improvement later in the year when soil moisture conditions will allow for it.

Continue inventory, monitoring and treatment of identified noxious weed infestations, for the management of the public lands in accordance with Idaho State Regulations.  Additional funds for the monitoring and treatment of noxious weeds will be requested in 2010 under the BAR.

Objectives: Objective is to identify all existing and new infestations of noxious weeds. New infestations will be treated and objective is to eliminate them from the treatment area. Existing noxious weeds will be treated to contain the infestation and prevent it from expanding on site.
Planned_Implementation: The proposal is to inventory and treat any noxious and/or invasive weeds within the burned area. Whitetop, rush skeletonweed are known to occur in the area, Scotch Thistle was identified during the ESR planning site tour. Inventory of weeds would occur both this fall (2010) and next spring (2011) and treatment of any infestations would occur over the next three springs and/or summers if necessary (2011, 2012, 2013). Weed control would occur using chemicals found on the BLM list of approved chemicals and applied either by ATV or backpack sprayer.
Actual_Implementation: FY12 ESR personnel inventoried the site on 06/15/12 and 07/15/2012. Multiple small Scotch thistle infestations were identified. Some were mechanically treated on 06/15/2012; the others were chemically treated in FY13. No other infestations were observed within the fire. FY13 Inventory and treatment completed by ESR/Weeds personnel and Elmore County Weed Control personnel May-June 2013.\r\nInventories were focused where probability for weed infestation was high and cursory elsewhere (see S5)
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Results
Isolated infestations of Scotch thistle with few plants per infestation were identified throughout the burn perimeter. Due to the small size of infestations, BLM personnel were able to mechanically treat them via hand pulling at the time of inventory. Although diffuse knapweed has been found along Bennett Mountain Road none has been found within the burn. Rush skeletonweed was also identified within the fire perimeter; plants were common in patches and widely distributed.
Conclusions
Although new infestations of Scotch thistle were inventoried each year, it is not expected to become a large problem. Diffuse and Russian knapweeds are also not expected to be a large problem going forward. Rush skeletonweed plants were too numerous in the vicinity (including private and state lands, and BLM managed lands surrounding the burn) to warrant chemical treatment. Further, the suite of biological control agents for rush skeletonweed (i.e., rust – Puccinia chondrillina; gall mite – Aceria chondrillae; gall midge – Cystiphora schmidti) is fully established throughout the region. Periodic inventory and chemical/mechanical treatment of Scotch thistle, diffuse knapweed, and Russian knapweed is recommended in the future.

Objectives: Objective: To inventory, detect and control any noxious weeds within the burn and map these sites for follow-up treatments during the following years.
Planned_Implementation: Conduct integrated weed management actions for noxious and invasive weed populations that are impacting or threatening GRSG habitat quality using a variety of eradication and control techniques including chemical, mechanical and other appropriate means.
Actual_Implementation: An aerial spraying contract was awarded and completed on approximately 9,696 acres (included IDL land), with Imazapic and Milestone in the fall of 2020.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
An aerial herbicide treatment consisting of Imazapic and Milestone was implemented on much of the burn in the fall of 2020 to reduce competition from cheatgrass (Figure 8). This chemical combination was recommend based upon past BLM success (Twin Falls District) with these chemicals at controlling cheatgrass. It is anticipated that the benefits from the herbicide application should last into the 2022 growing season. After that, reevaluation of the site would be required to determine the need for further treatments.

2021 Results: 
Benefits from the herbicide application were observed during 2021 field monitoring (Table 7). The herbicide combination was very effective at controlling cheatgrass as no germination was observed. Additionally, the herbicides were effective at controlling much of the skeletonweed. and areas where skeletonweed was observed was likely the result of application inconsistencies due to terrain and application skips. Reevaluation of the site in 2022 will determine the long-term efficacy of the herbicides and the need for further treatments.

2022 Results: 
Reevaluation of the site in 2022 determined that the long-term efficacy of the herbicides is limited to less than two years. Field assessments showed increase annual grass and noxious weed presence compared to the previous year’s data.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The entirety of the Horse Butte Fire area is identified as Important Habitat for greater sage-grouse (GRSG) and approximately 8,278 acres are identified as sage-grouse nesting/late brood-rearing habitat. The entire burn area is also identified as sage-grouse Potential Restoration Area, Type I: Perennial Grassland, which are sagebrush-limited areas characterized by perennial grass species composition which should provide suitable sage-grouse nesting habitat once sufficient sagebrush cover is re-established. In addition to GRSG the area is a designated big-game winter range and migration route priority habitat that is utilized by big-game species such as elk (Cervus canadensis), mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), and pronghorn (Antilocapra americana), as well as a host of sagebrush obligate species.
